desc:
You must swap the letters at exactly one pair of different positions i < j of the string s (you are not allowed to skip the swap, but the two swapped letters may be equal). Return true if the result can equal the string goal.

s = "ab",   goal = "ba"    result = true
s = "ab",   goal = "ab"    result = false  (a swap changes it)
s = "aab",  goal = "aab"   result = true   (swap the two a's)
s = "abc",  goal = "acd"   result = false
constraints: s and goal consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Different lengths can never match. Then think about where s and goal differ.
If they differ in exactly two positions, the swap must exchange those two letters. If they differ in one place, or in three or more, a single swap cannot repair them.
If the strings are already equal, the forced swap must not change anything, which is only possible when some letter occurs twice.
editorial: Split into cases by the set of positions where the strings differ. With exactly two differing positions a < b, the swap fixes the strings iff s[a] == goal[b] and s[b] == goal[a]. With exactly one differing position, no swap works (a swap changes two positions, or none). With three or more differing positions, one swap cannot repair them all.

With zero differing positions the swap has to leave s unchanged, which means swapping two equal letters, so we need a repeated letter. Since only 36 symbols exist, any string longer than 36 characters certainly has a repeat. Everything is one linear pass.
